pull.title: contrib: ci: Monitor Windows signing certificate expiry
pull.body:
Currently we have no automation in place to check that our code signing certificates are not expired or close to expiry. We have previously "relied on Release Candidates" as a dry-run for codesigners to realise that a certificate has expired and have time to fix it. "Noticing during RC cycle" also might not be appropriate in the future if we release more bugfix minor/patch releases on short notice.

In place of this process we can run a weekly CI job which will check the certificate's validity and open an issue when it passes an expiry threshold.

In this draft we only check the windows cert (as I couldn't find a mac one) and we set the alert threshold to 90 days.

When the threshold is passed, the job will open an issue in this repo (optionally tagging relevant key-holders).

events.body: The following sections might be updated with supplementary metadata relevant to reviewers and maintainers. ### External sites * Code coverage & benchmarks: https://corecheck.dev/bitcoin/bitcoin/pulls/36673 * Ralph review https://git.fish.foo/bitcoin/bitcoin/pulls/36673#author-ralph ### Reviews See [the guideline](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#code-review) and [AI policy](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/AI_POLICY.md) for information on the review process. | Type | Reviewers | | ---- | --------- | | Stale ACK | [achow101](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36673#issuecomment-6642802150) | If your review is incorrectly listed, please copy-paste <!--meta-tag:bot-skip--> into the comment that the bot should ignore.

I've tested a run in my fork [here](https://github.com/willcl-ark/bitcoin/actions/runs/40484898362/job/122124136348) with an increased threshold of 365 days to trigger posting an issue which was correctly opened [here](https://github.com/willcl-ark/bitcoin/issues/37).

> ... we set the alert threshold to 30 days.

What's the rationale for this length period?

> > ... we set the alert threshold to 30 days.
> 
> What's the rationale for this length period?

There is no current rationale for this, it's a placeholder for now. It depends I guess on the average lead-time to obtain updated keys.

> It depends I guess on the average lead-time to obtain updated keys.

The lead time has been anywhere between a couple days, to about 2.5 months, depending on whether a change of CA and signing org was necessary.

> The lead time has been anywhere between a couple days, to about 2.5 months, depending on whether a change of CA and signing org was necessary.

Bumped the placeholder example threshold to 90 days.
Alternatively, we could amend the release process as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36695#issuecomment-6505826743.

> Alternatively, we could amend the release process as suggested in [#36695 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36695#issuecomment-6505826743).

Yep! No skin off my back either way; happy with either approach.

> Alternatively, we could amend the release process as suggested in

Can you explain what that solves? The certs are constantly used to produce (point) releases, not just major releases, so *always* need to work (particularly in the case of expedited releases, like this week). 

A note in an issue telling someone to manually look at the cert at an arbitrary future time is not useful if we want to know the cert works for a deployment tomorrow.

I think the idea was to include a new section, which is either:

#### 2027-01-04 Update Windows signing cert 🚧

* Expires 2027-MM-DD


or:

#### 2027-01-04 Update Windows signing cert :heavy_check_mark: 

* Expires 2029-MM-DD, not needed


Maybe a script can be added for this to make it easier to run, if needed. Trusting the CI to create such an issue (which I presume happens less than once a year) seems more brittle? But no strong opinion.

> I think the idea was to include a new section, which is either:

Ok. I think the point of this PR is to try and move away from manual tasks that (hopefully) someone will remember to do, and more towards (automated) assurance that we can use the certs (my understanding is that the cert could also be revoked arbitrarily, along with normal expiration). Having this assurance would mean one less thing that an rc cycle needs to "check". Adding a note seems fine, but that seems to assume the cert is always valid?

I think we should also add a similar check for macOS code-signing, given that is more prone to breakage (needs manual intervention multiple time a year to accept updated T&Cs). An automated check makes more sense in this case, because the breakage is somewhat arbitrary.

> I think we should also add a similar check for macOS code-signing

To my knowledge the cert is not checked into this repo? but otherwise can trivially add the second check.

I am just a bit unsure if some random bash encoded in a string inside a yaml inside a mutable GHA VM inside some MS datacenter that requires a GHA write token to create an issue over the API is more reliable than the status quo. Again, no strong opinion, but the script should probably be stand-alone, so that it can be run locally?

> (my understanding is that the cert could also be revoked arbitrarily, along with normal expiration)

Would be nice to check for that. The CRL URL is embedded in the cert.

> I think we should also add a similar check for macOS code-signing,

The cert is not in the repo, so we cannot perform this check currently.

> given that is more prone to breakage (needs manual intervention multiple time a year to accept updated T&Cs). An automated check makes more sense in this case, because the breakage is somewhat arbitrary.

It's not clear to me whether that breakage is occurring during signing or notarization. Either way, I don't think we can have any automated check for that, unless CI were to also have a code signing private key and a notarization API key, which I think is inadvisable.

> Would be nice to check for that. The CRL URL is embedded in the cert.

Added a light check for revocation.

> I am just a bit unsure if some random bash encoded in a string inside a yaml inside a mutable GHA VM inside some MS datacenter that requires a GHA write token to create an issue over the API is more reliable than the status quo.

Moved this to a contrib script to it can be run manually (and in an automated CI job ;) )

While testing in my fork, I [got](https://github.com/hebasto/bitcoin/actions/runs/42366820166/job/128386510341):
```
Run status=0
  status=0
  ./contrib/devtools/check-code-signing-certificates.py > "$RUNNER_TEMP/certificate-report.txt" || status=$?
  cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/certificate-report.txt"
  if (( status == 1 )); then
    echo "warning=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  else
    exit "$status"
  fi
  shell: /usr/bin/bash --noprofile --norc -e -o pipefail {0}
  
Revocation check failed for contrib/windeploy/win-codesign.cert:
Unable to load CRL via CDP
40D7DD81DB7F0000:error:1E800075:HTTP routines:check_set_resp_len:max resp len exceeded:../crypto/http/http_client.c:491:length=188339, max=102400
40D7DD81DB7F0000:error:1E800067:HTTP routines:OSSL_HTTP_REQ_CTX_exchange:error receiving:../crypto/http/http_client.c:912:server=[http://crl3.digicert.com:80](http://crl3.digicert.com/)
C = US, ST = Delaware, L = Lewes, O = Bitcoin Core Code Signing LLC, CN = Bitcoin Core Code Signing LLC
error 3 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get certificate CRL
error contrib/windeploy/win-codesign.cert: verification failed
Error: Process completed with exit code 2.
```

> While testing in my fork, I [got](https://github.com/hebasto/bitcoin/actions/runs/42366820166/job/128386510341):

Thanks, reproduced with OpenSSL 3.0.13.

Its CRL downloader has a 100 KiB limit, so I updated the script to download separately and pass the file to OpenSSL for verification which mitigates.

committer will <will@256k1.dev> 1794311866 +0000

ci: Monitor Windows signing certificate expiry and

...revocation.

Check the signing certificate on master weekly so maintainers have time
to renew it before Windows release signing is affected. Open an issue
within 90 days of expiry, including certificate details and the checked
commit.

A signing certificate can also be revoked (before its expiry warning
window). Fetch and validate its CRL so the weekly monitor can report
confirmed revocation without treating network or verification failures
as certificate replacement alerts.

@@ -0,0 +1,72 @@
+# Copyright (c) 2026-present The Bitcoin Core developers
+# Distributed under the MIT software license, see the accompanying
+# file COPYING or https://opensource.org/license/mit.
+
+name: Code signing certificate
+on:
+  workflow_dispatch:
+  schedule:
+    # Mondays at 09:23 UTC.
+    - cron: '23 9 * * 1'
+
+permissions:
+  contents: read
+  issues: write
+
+concurrency:
+  group: code-signing-certificate
+
+jobs:
+  check-certificate:
+    if: github.repository == 'bitcoin/bitcoin'
+    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
+    timeout-minutes: 5
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
+        with:
+          ref: master
+          persist-credentials: false
+
+      - name: Check certificate expiry
+        env:
+          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
+          GH_REPO: bitcoin/bitcoin
+        shell: bash
+        run: |
+          CERT=contrib/windeploy/win-codesign.cert
+          WARNING_DAYS=90
+          # The first certificate in the PEM bundle is the code signing certificate.

There is not (nice question).

The only way I know to "check" which is which, without hardcoding, is to check `CA:FALSE` to at least rule out that its a cert authority.

I can push a change to this perhaps.
